Figure 4 depicts the difference between the federal and state minimum wage. A darker red shade represents a bigger negative difference between federal and state minimum wage. This indicates workers in that particular state are being underpaid according to what the federal government believes workers should be paid to have a minimum quality of life.

text:
The difference between state and federal minimum wage in 2020.
















Figure 5 depicts the state minimum wage across the United States, this time for the year of 2020. What is super surprising to me is that there are still certain states in the South that are not paying their workers a livable wage. The states of California, Washington, and the upper East Coast states are continually increasing their minimum wage to match what they believe will allow their residents to have a minimum quality of life. Notice how the states of Florida and Georgia have slightly increased their minimum wage, but certainly not enough where their residents and workers are able to have a quality of life.
Figure 6 depicts the difference between the federal minimum wage and the federal minimum wage. Again, the majority of states in the Southern region are underpaying their workers. Even though there is a federal minimum, those particular states are not matching it. This affects the quality of life of the residents who reside in those states. There seems to be a half and half split of whether or not states are paying their workers a livable wage. The purple shades indicates particular states where they are paying their workers above the federal minimum wage. While the states shaded in red indicate that those states are under paying their workers.

Background Information
For our final project in Data Science II, we are analyzing data found on the National Parks website, and joining it with other publicly available National Park data. Information we grabbed with the National Parks Service (NPS) API includes activities to do at each park, the address, and location, including coordinates and state. We joined this data set we created with data sets of visitors to each park and species that have been found in each of the parks.
With this project, our goal is to help plan future trips to recreational areas by showing when parks are busy, what there is to do there, their location and size, and fun wildlife that can be seen.

Conclusions

Our Findings
Our motivation for this project is exploring the National Parks. We were interested in knowing what one can do at each park, and what the park offers. This sparked our interest in finding out the types of activities offered throughout the park. From the National Parks API, we were able to grab the addresses for each of the state parks, and the list of activities that each park offers. In addition to the basic information that can be pulled from the National Parks website, we were interested in knowing what types of wildlife we would expect to see.
First, with our analysis of activities, we found that The Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve has the most number of activities offered, and Haleakala has the least. The distribution of activities at parks looks relatively normal, centered around 30 activities per park. Just a few popular activities we can see from the wordcloud include wildlife watching, hiking, different types of camping, boating, snowshoeing, and the junior ranger program.
With our map, we are able to see where parks are located across the country, and see what is close to us or in states we may want to visit. We are also able to see the size of parks, and which are smaller or larger. Clicking on a park shows the name, exact area, and address if we want to use that information to put into a map and see how far away it is.
On the species tab, we can see the most common species across all parks are various plants and birds. These are likely the species that have a wide range of habitats. With our interactive graph, users are able to input a park they potentially want to visit or are interested in, and can see which types of species are most commonly spotted in that park.
Lastly, we made two visitation tabs. From our first graph we find that the intermountain region sees the most amount of visitors to their national parks. The intermountain region includes parks like Yellowstone NP, Grand Canyon NP, and Zion NP. The region with the least amount of visitors is Alaska, which makes sense, as some of these parks are difficult to get to. For example, Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve has no roads to get to it, and if someone wants to visit, they must arrive by plane or hike. Our next graph shows the total number of visits throughout the year. The most popular month to visit a park is in the 7th month, or July. On the comparison tab, our plot is interactive, where the user can pick which parks they want to look at. They show visitation throughout the year. Users can choose a park they might want to visit, planning which time to go based on popular times, or when it would be less busy. The plot allows them to compare two parks at once.

title: Mini Project: Simulations
text:
We are interested in seeing if gas prices changed over time. Since the worlds economy is ever changing, I thought it would be interesting to analyze gas prices. Living in the United States, we only hear about the outrages gas prices within the states; however, how are other countries dealing with such changes, if there are any to begin with. I was curious to see if the changing gas prices were that drastic as well. We begin by importing the Ontario gas prices dataset. I wanted to explore how gas prices vary within a two very different regions of the same city. Here, my analysis involves the difference of two means. So I tidied my dataset such that the column date was a binary variable, which took on the values of “yes” or “no”, representing if the observation year was pre_2010 or not.

#initial data cleaning
ontario_gas <- read_csv("~/Desktop/SDSProjects/mary_wu.github.io/Ontario_Fuel_Prices_1990_2023.csv") |>
  select(Date, `Toronto West/Ouest`, `Toronto East/Est`) |> 
  rename(`east_toronto` = `Toronto East/Est`, `date` = `Date`) |>
  mutate(date = year(ymd(date)),
         pre_2010 = ifelse(date < 2010, "Yes", "No"),
         east_toronto = as.numeric(east_toronto)) |>
  select(-date) |>
  drop_na() 

After we created the ontario_gas dataset, let us make sure that we are able to grab the mean gas prices of pre_2010. Notice the output is a 2x2 tibble. It shows us the mean gas prices from the years of 1990 to 2009, and the mean gas prices from the years of 2010 to 2023.

ontario_gas |>
  group_by(pre_2010) |> 
  summarise(mean_gas = mean(east_toronto))

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  pre_2010 mean_gas
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 No          106. 
2 Yes          63.2


From this output, it seems like before 2010, the mean gas price in east was around 63.2 Canadian dollars, and gas prices after 2010 was around 106 Canadian dollars.
Now that we verified that our new dataset works, let us create a function such that we are able to easily explore the different years and regions within Ontario. However, remember that in this simulation, we are only interested in the regions of West and East Toronto.

mean_ontario_gas <- function(gas_vec, year_vec) {
  mean_tbl <- 
  ontario_gas |> 
  group_by({{year_vec}}) |>
  summarise(mean_gas = mean({{gas_vec}}))

  observed_diff <- mean_tbl[[2]][1] - mean_tbl[[2]][2]
}

Note that the difference in means between the two time periods is 43.10 Canadian dollars. This indicates that after 2010, the gas prices in East Toronto is 43.10 Canadian dollars more expensive than gas prices before the years of 2010.
Now that we know the actual difference in gas prices, let us run a simulation to see if there is an actual difference in the mean prices between the two time periods. In addition, it will help us in assessing our model’s accuracy. Because real-world scenarios might not adhere to statistical assumptions or distributions, it is important to run statistical analysis to analyse to see if there is a statistical significance. Here, we are running our simulation 1000 times. Note that we need to shuffle the data to see if the results happen by chance, or if there is an actual relationship between the variables.

simulated_diffs1 <- vector("double", 1000)

for(i in 1:1000) {
  mean_tbl <- ontario_gas |> 
    mutate(pre_2010 = sample(pre_2010)) |> 
    group_by(pre_2010) |>
    summarise(mean_gas = mean(east_toronto))
   
  simulated_diffs1[[i]] <- mean_tbl[[2]][1] - mean_tbl[[2]][2]
}

Once we have the simulated differences, we need to plot out simulated data against our observed difference. Remember that our observed difference in the mean gas prices is 42.8 Canadian dollars. By plotting a histogram, we are able to compare our simulated data against our observed mean difference.

null_world <- tibble(simulated_diffs1 = simulated_diffs1)

ggplot(null_world, aes(x = simulated_diffs1)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_ontario_gas(east_toronto, pre_2010), color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Simulated Difference in Gas Prices",
       subtitle = "In East Toronto",
       x = "Simulated Differences",
       y = "Count")

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









Note that we plotted the observed difference as the horizontal red line. The histogram represents the values we received when we ran our simulations. Notice how the red line is super far away from our simulated data. This indicates that there is significant evidence that there is a difference between the mean prices of gas prices between the two time periods (pre 2010 and post 2010).
Now that we ran our simulation and plotted it on a histogram, let us also perform a statistical test to see how accurate our simulation was. Note that because we are interested in the difference of two means, we have to run a t-test.

t_test_result <- t.test(ontario_gas$east_toronto ~ ontario_gas$pre_2010)

t_test_result


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  ontario_gas$east_toronto by ontario_gas$pre_2010
t = 57.486, df = 5829.3, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group No and group Yes is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 41.62830 44.56775
sample estimates:
 mean in group No mean in group Yes 
        106.33840          63.24037 


From our t-test, we have a p-value of 2.2e-16, which agrees with our results of our simulation. There is significant evidence that there is a difference in the true means of gas prices between the two time periods of post 2010 and pre 2010.

}

In class we have gone through the process of a creating a classifier to distinguish a 2 from 7 by using some predefined features, which correspond to the proportion of dark pixels in different quadrants of an image. Is there a solid way to classify between the numbers? It might be easy to distinguish these two numbers if it were just one person’s handwriting. However, we want to create a classifier such that we are able to distinguish between these two numbers given a large set of handwritten numbers. With everyone having their own distinct way of writing, how are we able to create a general classification such that we are able to distinguish between the 10 numbers? We are interested in distinguishing between the digits of 5 and 7. To do this, we have to create a classifier, which distinguishes a 5 from 7 by using some predefined features, which corresponds to the proportion of dark pixels of an image. In this challenge we will be using the mnist dataset to create an end-to-end classifier that distinguishes between two digits 5 and 7.


We begin our analysis with importing the mnist dataset, which includes 60,000 rows, which corresponds to 60,000 different handwritten digits. However, this takes up a lot of memory, so we decided to include the first 1000 rows in our initial analysis. Note how we use the function slide_head(n=1000) to grab the first 1000 rows of the mnist dataset. We call this new dataset mnist_5_7.
Our new dataset of mnist5_7 has 1000 observations and 875 variables. The first variable, digit, corresponds to what number is represented. The rest of the columns, V1:V784 correspond to the gray-scale values of each of the pixels from a 28 by 28 image.



We create a function that will allow us to visualize one of the rows of our dataset:

plot_digit <- function(row) {

    select(-digit)|>
    as.numeric()|>
    matrix(nrow = 28)

}

The function works by removing the first column (digit), then converting the row into a vector, and then into 28 by 28 matrix. Finally we use the image() function in R to plot the resulting (rotated) matrix. We use this function below to explore the images corresponding to the 16th, 12th, 30th and and 60th digit from our data set to understand the variations in the shape.:

plot_digit(mnist5_7[66,])











A region of an image can be defined by a 28 by 28 matrix of 0s and 1s, which can be represented as a text file where the rows are separated by “,” and where columns occur in different lines. For our regions selection, we wanted to be more creative and at the same time efficient so to maximize the area covered by both our digits 5 and 7 but minimizing the overlap. For region1, which represents digit 5, we’ve created a shape that intriguingly resembles the digit 7. This is a creative approach on our side because while the digit 5 has a different structure, by using the negative space of 7 we’re effectively creating a complementary shape that does not overlap with the actual 7 digit. Whereas, For region2, representing digit 7 to take a staggered form that extends diagonally across the matrix we aimed at creating a boomerang looking shape or a staircase shape to cover the distinctive features of the digit 7, like its horizontal line on the top and the angular line descending to the right. This pattern would occupy spaces that are less likely to be filled by the digit 5, which typically has a horizontal line at the lower part and a curve at the top right. Inside the function, this table is converted into a matrix and the values are multiplied by 128, suggesting that the binary 0 or 1 values in tbl are scaled up to create a grayscale image with pixel values of either 0 or 128. Then, the function image is used to display this matrix. However, before the matrix is passed to the image function, it is transposed using the t() function and then flipped along the vertical axis (as indicated by the [28:1] indexing), which effectively rotates the image for proper orientation. The purpose of this function is to plot the region of a digit from a 28 by 28 matrix, where the digit’s shape is represented in a format suitable for image display in R.

  image(t(digit_mat)[,28:1]) #Plot the image making sure is rotated
}

plot_region(region2)








Now, given an image and a region, we would like to calculate the proportion of dark pixels of the image in the region. We can do that using the function calc_prop(). The calc_prop function is designed to determine the proportion of dark pixels within a certain region of an image. It takes a predefined region matrix where the value 1 indicates the relevant region, and a row vector representing pixel data from an image. The region matrix is rotated and flipped to align with the MNIST dataset’s image orientation. Next, the row vector is converted into numerical form, if it isn’t already, and reshaped into a 28x28 pixel matrix that represents the image, known as digit_mat. The function then identifies which pixels fall within the specified region and assesses whether these pixels are dark based on a threshold value (greater than 20 out of 255 in grayscale). It counts the dark pixels and calculates their proportion within the selected region, which is then returned as the output. This method is generally useful in image processing tasks where the density of dark pixels within specific areas needs to be analyzed, such as in handwriting recognition here.

calc_prop <- function (region, row) {
  # Rotate "region" so is in same order as mnist images
  region <- t(as.matrix(region))[,28:1]
  # Take row from mnist and transform into a "digit" matrix
  digit_mat <-  row |>
    as.numeric()|>
    matrix(nrow = 28)
  # Find positions of pixels from "region"
  pos = (region==1)
  # Subset "digit" to the positions and count dark pixels (grey>20)
  dark = digit_mat[pos]>20 
  # Return proportion of dark pixels of "image" in "region"
  return(sum(dark)/sum(pos))
}

We calculate the proportion of dark pixels across the two areas of interest (see section The proportion of dark pixels ..) using the mnist5_7 dataset and create a new tibble features_tbl that contains four columns: id, which is a consecutive number from 1 to 1000, digit which is a factor corresponding to our digit type, prop1 which corresponds to the proportion of dark pixels for region1, and prop2 which is the proportion of dark pixels for region2. The dataset is saved as mnist5_7.features.csv.

features_tbl <- mnist5_7|>
  rowwise()|>
  mutate(
    prop1=calc_prop(region1,c_across(V1:V784)),
         prop2=calc_prop(region2,c_across(V1:V784))) |>
  select(digit,prop1, prop2) |>
  ungroup() |>
  tibble::rowid_to_column("ID")




The following code allows us to visualize the spread of values for “prop1” and “prop2” for the digits 5 and 7. We accomplish this by creating a ggplot using “features_tbl” as the data. Within this ggplot, we place the values of “prop1” on the x-axis and the values of “prop2” on the y-axis, and we use colors to differentiate the 5’s and 7’s. Finally, we use geom_point() to create a scatter plot of the data.

features_tbl |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop1, y = prop2, color = digit)) +
  geom_point()








The scatter plot visualizes two variables, prop1 and prop2, which represent the proportion of dark pixels in the predefined regions for the digits 5 and 7. The blue points represent 7, and the red points represent 5. The separation between the clusters of blue and red points suggests that prop1 and prop2 are effective features for differentiating between the two digit types. Most of the blue points (for 7) are grouped together, as are the red points (for the 5), with a relatively clear boundary between them. This clustering indicates a good level of distinction between the digit types based on these features, which will be hopefully advantageous when developing our models. However, there are some overlapping areas where red and blue points are mixed, indicating areas where the digit representations share similar proportions of dark pixels for 5’s and 7’s. As such, our models will likely have more difficulty classifying digits in these areas.

Model creation, optimization and selection
Create at least two different models for distinguishing the two different digit types using your two defined features. If the models have parameters (for example the k in KNN) make sure to find the optimal values of the parameters. Calculate the accuracy of each model in your dataset, select the model with the highest accuracy, and calculate the confusion matrix for the model with the highest accuracy


We’ve chosen two contrasting models: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Logistic Regression. The rationale for this choice lies in the complementary nature of the decision boundaries that each model constructs.KNN makes custom-fit decisions by closely examining its nearest data points. Its ability to capture the nuanced, subtle patterns in the dataset by considering the proximity of its neighbors makes it an excellent candidate for when the relationships within the data are complex and interwoven. Logistic Regression, on the other hand, takes on the role of a cartographer, drawing straight-line boundaries to divide the dataset into classes. Its strength lies in its straightforward approach, making it ideal for situations where a linear relationship does a good job of separating the classes. Choosing these two models allows us to explore and understand our dataset from two different perspectives: one that is intricately detailed and another that is elegantly straightforward. By comparing their performance, we hope to gain a deeper insight into the nature of our data and can make a more informed decision on which model best captures the underlying relationships between our variables.




The following code creates our multinomial logistic regression model. The model attempts to classify the digit based on the values of prop1 and prop2, and it is trained on the training data we created in the previous section. After creating the model, we also have code that tests the accuracy of the model, including the overall accuracy as well as the individual accuracies for 5’s and 7’s.

KNN


For our second model we developed a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification model using auxiliary functions and the determination of the optimal number of neighbors (K) to ensure the best possible model accuracy. Firstly, we established auxiliary functions that allow us to generate and assess the KNN model systematically. The create_knn function is designed to take in a specified number of neighbors (K) and a dataset, using these parameters to build a KNN model for classification purposes by we specifying the KNN algorithm, the mode of the model (classification), and the formula that describes the relationship between predictors and outcome digit here. A function named calc_accuracy, which serves to evaluate the performance of our KNN model. It predicts the classes for a given dataset and then compares these predictions to the true labels to calculate the accuracy of the model. The following code creates a KNN model.



#KNN model generalized
# Creates a KNN classification model
create_knn <- function(k, tbl) {
  knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = k) %>%
    set_mode("classification") %>%
    set_engine("kknn")

  knn_recipe <- recipe(digit ~ prop1 + prop2, data=tbl)
  
  knn_wflow <- workflow() %>%
    add_recipe(knn_recipe) %>%
    add_model(knn_spec)

KNN Accuracy function –auxiliary function

calc_accuracy <- function(knn_model, tbl) {
  predictions <- predict(knn_model, tbl)$.pred_class
  true_labels <- tbl$digit
  mean(predictions == true_labels)
}

The accuracy of this retrained model is 60%, with 64% accuracy for 5’s, 75% accuracy for 7’s, and 42.7% accuracy for 6’s. The confusion matrix for the (KNN) prediction of digits 5, 6, and 7 above suggests that there is a notable level of confusion between the digits 5 and 6. The model has misclassified the digit 5 as 6 a total of 24 times, and similarly, the digit 6 as 5 a total of 24 times, which is the highest off-diagonal count observed in the matrix. This pattern of confusion could potentially be attributed to the similar shapes and strokes involved in writing these two digits. For instance, both digits have a round component—the lower half of ‘5’ and 6’. When written quickly or with a particular style, the distinction between the two can become blurred. Additionally, the top part of a ‘5’ can sometimes resemble the loop of a ‘6’, especially if the ‘5’ is not properly closed or the ‘6’ is loosely written. Also, it is worth noting that 6’s tend to get misclassified more often than either 5’s or 7’s. This is because 6’s are often misclassified as either 5’s or 7’s, while 5’s are not often misclassified as 7’s and 7’s are not often misclassified as 5’s. This is likely because we were not considering 6’s when creating our regions and were instead aiming to create regions that would distinguish between 5’s and 7’s well (which the new model still appears to do fairly well).
